title: Cancelectomy
excerpt: Sometimes the words people invent at work reveal more about a profession—and the people behind it – than any textbook ever could.
body:
Every profession has its own language.

Lawyers have expressions that make no sense to anyone outside the courtroom. Pilots speak in abbreviations. IT professionals casually suggest that you "turn it off and on again."

Surgery has cancelectomy.

It's not a real medical procedure, although on particularly busy mornings, many of us secretly wish it were.

If you've never worked in surgery, let me explain.

Every morning begins the same way. Someone updates the whiteboard with the day's schedule. Every procedure, every surgeon, every patient is listed there. Before anyone has finished their coffee, the entire team has already walked over to look at it.

That whiteboard tells you almost everything you need to know about your day.

A board with a comfortable number of cases usually earns a quiet nod of approval. A board filled from top to bottom, with emergency cases squeezed into every available space, has a different effect. You don't even need to say anything. Everyone does the same silent calculation: How many surprises will today have in store? When are we going to eat? Are we leaving on time?

And then someone says it.

"Maybe we'll get a little cancelectomy today."

Nobody means they hope a patient becomes too sick for surgery. Nobody wants anyone's plans to fall apart. Quite the opposite. Every cancellation usually represents someone whose operation had to be postponed, often because of circumstances nobody wanted.

The joke isn't about patients.

It's about capacity.

It's about the tiny, guilty feeling of relief that appears when an impossibly full day suddenly becomes... slightly less impossible.

Healthcare professionals rarely admit that feeling out loud because it sounds wrong. We chose professions built around helping others. Relief can easily be mistaken for indifference.

But the two are not the same.

Feeling relieved doesn't mean you care less. More often, it means you've been carrying more than your nervous system was ever designed to carry. After hours of making decisions, solving problems, adapting to the unexpected, and giving your full attention to everyone else, even one cancelled case can feel like someone quietly handed you back a few minutes to breathe.

That's one of the things I find fascinating about workplace humor. The funniest jokes often reveal the hardest truths. They become a safe way of saying things that would otherwise feel uncomfortable. They allow people to acknowledge something difficult without turning it into a dramatic conversation.

Cancelectomy isn't really about cancelled surgeries.

It's about the invisible weight that healthcare professionals carry every day while continuing to show up, care deeply, and do their best for every patient. It's about trying to do your best for every patient while quietly hoping the day gives you just enough room to breathe. Sometimes the healthiest thing a team can do is laugh together at a word that doesn't exist.

Because sometimes one made-up word tells you more about a profession than an entire textbook ever could.
